opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the key idea is what we call rapid motor adaptation. Rather than training one rigid controller for one environment, we train the policy in simulation across a huge variety of conditions: different friction, payloads, terrain heights, motor strengths, and so on. During training the policy has access to these environment parameters, and it learns to compress them into a small latent vector, which you can think of as a summary of "what kind of world am I in right now."

The catch is that in the real world the robot doesn't get those parameters handed to it. Nobody tells it, "you're now on wet grass with friction coefficient 0.4." So we train a second module, an adaptation module, that estimates that latent vector from the recent history of the robot's own states and actions. If I command my legs to do something and the body responds differently than expected, say my foot slips or sinks, that discrepancy is informative. Within a fraction of a second, the adaptation module updates its estimate of the environment, and the base policy conditions on that estimate and changes its behavior accordingly.

So it's a single policy, but it's not a fixed behavior. It's more like the policy has an internal sense of the world that keeps getting revised. That's quite analogous to what we do as humans. When you step onto ice, you don't consciously compute a friction coefficient. Your body notices that things feel different and your gait changes almost immediately. You shorten your stride, lower your center of mass. We wanted the robot to have that same kind of fast, implicit adaptation.

What I find interesting is that this happens without any explicit model of terrain categories. We never tell the robot "this is sand, this is stairs." The relevant distinctions emerge because they matter for control. And later, when we added vision, the story got richer: the robot can anticipate terrain before stepping on it, rather than only reacting after contact. But the proprioceptive adaptation remains the foundation. It's what lets the robot recover when its predictions are wrong, and in the real world, they often are.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot is never told terrain categories such as “sand” or “stairs” and that relevant distinctions emerge through control, communicating that adaptation does not depend on programmed terrain-specific rules.

r002.rationale: It explains that an adaptation module estimates the environment from recent robot states and actions, and that the walking policy uses this estimate to change its behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the first thing to say is that it's a single policy, one neural network, trained entirely in simulation, and then deployed on the real robot without any further fine-tuning. The question of how it adapts is really the heart of what we were trying to understand.

The key idea we call rapid motor adaptation, or RMA. During training in simulation, we have access to things the real robot will never be able to measure directly: the friction of the ground, the mass it's carrying, the stiffness of the terrain, whether a leg is slightly damaged. We train a base policy that takes in the robot's proprioception, so the joint angles, joint velocities, body orientation, and also takes in a compact latent vector that encodes those privileged environment properties. So in simulation the policy learns to walk well given knowledge of the terrain.

Then there's a second network, an adaptation module, which has to infer that latent vector purely from the recent history of the robot's own sensors and actions. The intuition is very simple. If I command my joints to move a certain way and they respond differently from what I expected, that mismatch tells me something about the world. If I push and the ground gives, it's soft. If my foot slips, friction is low. Humans do this constantly and unconsciously. You step onto ice and within a stride or two your gait has changed, not because you looked at the ice but because your body felt the slip.

So at deployment, the adaptation module is running continuously, looking at the last half second or so of experience, estimating the environment, and the base policy conditions on that estimate. There's no explicit terrain classifier, no labels like "sand" or "grass." It's a continuous latent space, and the robot adapts in a fraction of a second as conditions change under it.

What I find most interesting is that we didn't program any of these adaptations. Nobody wrote a rule that says lift your feet higher in tall grass. That emerged because in simulation we randomized over a huge range of terrains and payloads, and the only way to succeed across all of them was to learn to infer and adapt. In some sense the policy learned a little model of physics, implicitly, as a means to an end.

I'd also add a note of humility. We can probe the latent and see that it correlates with friction or payload, so we have some interpretability. But I wouldn't claim we fully understand everything the network has learned. There's a lot going on in those weights that we can only characterize behaviorally, by watching what the robot does when we put it on a new surface.

r001.rationale: The response says the adaptations were not programmed as rules and gives “lift your feet higher in tall grass” as an example of a rule nobody wrote.

r002.rationale: It explains that an adaptation module estimates terrain and other environmental properties from recent sensor and action history, and the walking policy conditions on that estimate.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a feedback policy, rather than a collection of separate walking routines. The robot senses how its body is moving and what is happening at its feet, and the policy uses that information to decide what to do next. So a single policy doesn’t mean a single fixed pattern of motion. Different conditions produce different actions.

If a foot encounters the ground earlier than expected, or slips, that changes the feedback, and the subsequent actions can compensate. It need not explicitly say, “This is gravel,” or, “This is a slope.” What matters is whether it has learned to respond appropriately to the consequences of that terrain. And that adaptation has limits: a single policy is not a guarantee that it can handle every surface.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback policy rather than separate walking routines and says it need not explicitly identify terrain, conveying that adaptation does not depend on programmed terrain-specific rules.

r002.rationale: It says sensed body and foot feedback changes subsequent actions, but does not describe an internal estimate of external terrain conditions guiding those changes.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a single policy doesn’t mean a single fixed gait. It means a single rule for choosing actions based on what the robot is experiencing. As the terrain changes, the robot’s observations change, and the same policy can produce different behavior.

For example, on slippery ground, the useful response may be different from what you want on uneven ground. The robot can use its recent experience—how its feet move, how its body responds—to infer something about those conditions. It doesn’t necessarily have to label the terrain explicitly. What matters is that this information changes the actions it takes.

So the adaptation is in the relationship between sensing and action, rather than in switching between a collection of separately programmed walking behaviors.

r001.rationale: It contrasts sensing and action with switching among separately programmed behaviors, but does not clearly rule out terrain-specific if-then rules within the single policy.

r002.rationale: It says the robot uses recent experience to infer terrain conditions and that this information changes its actions.
